options.text: The vertical axis starts at $70$ instead of $0$
The bars are different colours
options.why: No colour difference is used, and colour would not change the numerical scale.

options.text: The days are shown in time order
options.why: Putting Saturday before Sunday is accurate and does not exaggerate the values.

options.text: The two bars have equal widths
options.why: Equal bar widths are a fair feature, not the source of the exaggeration.

questions.solution_text: The axis begins at $70$, so the small increase from $72$ to $80$ occupies most of the graph height.

options.text: Equal increases of $5$ use unequal vertical gaps
The axis begins at $0$
options.why: Starting a bar-graph axis at zero is fair and is not the problem shown.

options.text: The categories use words rather than numbers
options.why: Text labels correctly identify categories and do not affect the numerical scale.

options.text: The bars are separated by a gap
options.why: Gaps between category bars are expected and do not make the scale uneven.

questions.solution_text: The value increases are all $5$, but the vertical gaps are $1$, then $2$, then $1$ units. The scale is uneven.

options.text: The bagel bar is much wider than the roll bar
Both bars reach $6$
options.why: Equal heights correctly represent the equal values and are not misleading.

options.text: The axis uses intervals of $2$
options.why: A consistent many-to-one scale of two is valid and evenly spaced.

options.text: The graph includes a title
options.why: A clear title helps identify the data and does not distort the comparison.

questions.solution_text: Only bar height should represent the value. The unequal widths make the bagel bar's area look much larger despite equal values.

options.text: $8$ customers
$4$ customers
options.why: Counts four vertical drawing units but ignores that each unit represents two customers.

options.text: $160$ customers
options.why: Gives Saturday's total instead of subtracting Friday's $152$ customers.

options.text: $312$ customers
options.why: Adds the two daily totals instead of calculating the increase.

questions.solution_text:
Friday is $152$ and Saturday is $160$.
$160-152=8$
The increase is $8$ customers.

questions.question_text: A fair replacement is needed for a bar graph whose axis starts at $90$, whose tick gaps are uneven and whose bars have different widths. Which replacement fixes all three problems?

options.text: Start at $0$, use equal value intervals, and make all bars equal width
Start at $90$, use equal value intervals, and make all bars equal width
options.why: Fixes spacing and widths but keeps the truncated axis that exaggerates differences.

options.text: Start at $0$, keep uneven intervals, and make all bars equal width
options.why: Fixes the baseline and widths but leaves unequal value changes at equal-looking gaps.

options.text: Start at $0$, use equal intervals, and widen the largest-value bar
options.why: Fixes the axis but still lets bar width exaggerate one category.

questions.solution_text: A fair column graph starts at $0$, uses even scale intervals and gives every bar the same width.

questions.question_text: An advert says sales ‘nearly tripled’ because a graph's second bar looks almost three times as tall. The printed values are $196$ and $204$, and the axis begins at $192$. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The claim is false; sales increased by only $8$
The claim is true because $204$ is nearly three times $196$
options.why: Accepts the visual impression even though three times $196$ would be $588$.

options.text: The claim is true because the second bar is taller
options.why: Treats any increase in bar height as proof of tripling without comparing actual values.

options.text: The claim is false; sales decreased by $8$
options.why: Subtracts in the wrong direction even though the value rises from $196$ to $204$.

questions.solution_text:
$204-196=8$
Sales increased by only $8$; the truncated axis creates the exaggerated appearance.
